vignette:
Meera has always known the language of the land. For over forty years, the half-acre plot behind her home has been her domain, a place of tireless work but also of deep, quiet satisfaction. She knew the exact day to turn the soil for the winter gourds, the precise scent of the air when the monsoon was about to break, and the particular weight of a perfectly ripe mango in her palm. Her husband, Sameer, would often say she didn't just work the land; she conversed with it. That conversation stopped nine months ago.

It was an evening in late autumn, the sun bleeding into the horizon, casting long shadows from the jackfruit trees. She had stayed later than usual, wanting to finish staking the last row of tomato saplings. Sameer was in the village, picking up supplies. The air was cool and carried the familiar, comforting scent of damp earth and night-blooming jasmine. She was alone, but she had been alone in these fields thousands of times. It had never felt like a danger.

She doesn't talk about the specifics of what happened next, not in a linear way. The memory doesn't live in her mind as a story, but as a series of punishing sensory fragments. The rough bark of the tree against her back. The acrid smell of sweat and cheap tobacco. The weight, immense and suffocating, that stole the air from her lungs. The chirping of the cicadas, a sound she once found peaceful, which now seems to mock her, a frantic, high-pitched alarm that never ceases.

She remembers walking back to the house in the dark, her sari torn at the hem. She scrubbed her skin raw in the washroom, the water running cold, but she could not wash away the feeling of being soiled from the inside out. When Sameer returned, she was in bed, feigning sleep. She has been feigning something ever since.

The woman who once rose before the sun to greet her fields now dreads the light of day. The work, once a source of pride, is now a minefield of triggers. The smell of turned earth can send a wave of nausea through her, her body tensing as if bracing for an impact. She can no longer work alone. She insists Sameer stay within her line of sight, a demand that has sown a quiet confusion and resentment between them. He sees her fear but doesn't know its name, and she cannot bring herself to give it one. To speak it would be to make it irrevocably real, a stain on their family she feels she alone must bear.

Sleep offers no refuge. She often jolts awake, her heart hammering against her ribs, the phantom weight pressing down on her. She lies still in the dark, listening to her husband's steady breathing, and feels an ocean of distance from him, from the woman she used to be. During the day, a thick fog of shame settles over her. She finds herself staring at her hands, the same strong, capable hands that have planted and harvested for decades, and sees them as weak, as having failed to protect her.

Her world has shrunk to the four walls of her house. The vibrant community she was once a part of now feels threatening. A man's voice raised in the lane outside, the sudden appearance of a stranger at the gate, even a shadow falling over her unexpectedly can make her flinch, her breath catching in her throat. She feels like a ghost in her own life, watching her husband eat the food she cooked without tasting it, listening to her grandchildren's laughter as if from behind a thick wall of glass. The land lies fallow at the far end of the property, the weeds slowly reclaiming the patch of earth where she was last truly herself.
